title: Conditionals
description: Learn conditionals for Grade 8: zero, first, second and third conditionals plus mixed conditionals, alternatives to 'if', and inversion — with bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: The Four Conditional Types
topics.concept:
Type 0 (Zero) — facts: something always true. If + present, present.
If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.

Type 1 — real future: a likely situation and its result. If + present, will + V1.
If it rains, we will cancel the match.

Type 2 — unreal present/future: imaginary or unlikely now. If + past, would + V1.
If I won the lottery, I would buy a house. (Use were for all subjects: If I were you…)

Type 3 — unreal past: something that did not happen, often a regret. If + past perfect, would have + V3.
If she had studied, she would have passed.

examples.problem: Which type? If I were taller, I would play basketball.
examples.solution: Type 2 — an unreal present situation (I'm not taller). Note 'were' for all subjects.

examples.problem: Complete (Type 3): If he ___ (leave) earlier, he ___ (catch) the train.
examples.solution: had left … would have caught — an unreal past (he didn't leave earlier).

recap: Type 1: if + present, will + V1 (real future)
Type 2: if + past, would + V1 (unreal present; use 'were')
Type 3: if + past perfect, would have + V3 (unreal past)

topics.title: Mixed Conditionals, Alternatives & Inversion
topics.concept:
A mixed conditional joins a past condition to a present result (Type 3 if-clause + Type 2 main clause):

  • If I had taken the job (past), I would be rich now (present).

Alternatives to 'if':

  • unless = if not — Unless you hurry, you will be late.
  • provided / providing that, as long as, on condition that add a strict condition.

Formal inversion drops 'if' and moves the auxiliary to the front:

  • Were I rich, I would help. (= If I were rich…)
  • Had she known, she would have come. (= If she had known…)
  • Should you need help, call me. (= If you should need help…)

examples.problem: Rewrite with 'unless': If you don't study, you will fail.
examples.solution: Unless you study, you will fail. — 'unless' = 'if … not'.

examples.problem: Make it a mixed conditional: I didn't sleep well, so I am tired now.
examples.solution: If I had slept well, I would not be tired now.

recap: Mixed: if + past perfect (past) , would + V1 (present result)
'unless' = if not; 'provided/as long as' add a strict condition
Formal inversion: Were I…, Had she…, Should you… (drop 'if')

Use alternatives to 'if' (unless, provided, as long as)
Recognise the formal inversion of conditionals

intro.en: A conditional sentence talks about a condition and its result — "If X happens, then Y follows." The trick is that English uses different tense patterns depending on how real or likely the condition is. Get the pattern right and you can talk about facts, possibilities, dreams and regrets.
intro.hi: शर्तवाचक वाक्य (conditional) किसी शर्त और उसके परिणाम की बात करता है — "If X हो, तो then Y होगा।" मुख्य बात यह है कि अंग्रेज़ी अलग-अलग tense pattern प्रयोग करती है — यह इस पर निर्भर करता है कि शर्त कितनी वास्तविक या संभव है। सही pattern से आप तथ्य, संभावनाएँ, सपने और पछतावे — सब व्यक्त कर सकते हैं।

real_life.situation:
You weigh up a decision:

You: If it rains, I'll stay home. If I were rich, I'd travel the world. If I had studied medicine, I would have become a doctor.
real_life.why: Three conditions, three levels of reality: a real future possibility (Type 1), an unreal present dream (Type 2), and an impossible past regret (Type 3). The verb forms — not the word 'if' — tell us which is which.

rule_box.html:
TypeIf-clauseMain clauseMeaning
0presentpresentfact / always true
1presentwill + V1real future
2pastwould + V1unreal present
3past perfectwould have + V3unreal past
rule_box.formula: Type 1: If + present, will + V1 · Type 2: If + past, would + V1 · Type 3: If + had + V3, would have + V3
rule_box.example: If you heat ice, it melts (0). If it rains, I'll stay (1). If I were you, I'd go (2). If I had known, I'd have come (3).

common_mistakes.wrong: If I will see him, I will tell him.
common_mistakes.right: If I see him, I will tell him.
common_mistakes.note: The if-clause of Type 1 takes the present, not 'will'.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I was you, I would go. (formal)
common_mistakes.right: If I were you, I would go.
common_mistakes.note: Use 'were' for all subjects in Type 2.

common_mistakes.wrong: If she had studied, she would pass.
common_mistakes.right: If she had studied, she would have passed.

common_mistakes.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, you'll be late.
common_mistakes.right: Unless you hurry, you'll be late.
common_mistakes.note: 'unless' already means 'if not' — don't add another negative.

reading.passage: "If you water plants regularly, they grow," said the gardener. "If it rains tonight, I won't need to water them tomorrow. But if I were a richer man, I would install a sprinkler system. If I had planted those seeds last spring, we would have flowers now. Unless we protect this garden, it will not survive."

questions.q: Find the zero conditional and explain why it is used.
questions.answer: "If you water plants regularly, they grow" — it states a general fact (present, present).

questions.q: Identify the mixed conditional and its meaning.
questions.answer: "If I had planted those seeds last spring, we would have flowers now" — past condition, present result.

questions.q: Rewrite the 'unless' sentence using 'if … not'.
questions.answer: If we do not protect this garden, it will not survive.
